title: Exploring the Investigative World of Science

learn.hook: Why does curd set faster in May than in January? You can find out the way a scientist would: watch, wonder, guess, test and check!
points: Science begins with an observation, something we notice using our senses or instruments, and a question about it.
A hypothesis is a possible answer to the question that can be tested, for example 'Warmth helps milk turn into curd faster.'
We test a hypothesis with an experiment or careful observations, and we record what happens as data, often in a table.
We analyse the data to see if it supports the hypothesis. If it does not, we change the hypothesis and test again. That is not failure, it is learning.
Good scientists repeat their tests, report honestly and share their results so that others can check them.

example.q: Think it through: Aarav says, 'Plants on our balcony grow taller than the plants inside the room because they get more sunlight.' How can he investigate this?
steps: Observation: balcony plants look taller.
Hypothesis: more sunlight makes the plants grow taller.
Experiment: grow two similar pots of the same plant, one in sunlight and one in a dim corner, with the same soil and the same water.
Record the height of each plant every few days in a table.
Analyse: if the sunny plant grows taller, the data supports his hypothesis.
example.answer: He should make a testable hypothesis, run a fair experiment with two similar pots, record heights, and compare the data before concluding.

learn.reallife: Doctors testing a new medicine, farmers trying a new seed variety and ISRO teams testing rocket parts all follow these same steps of investigation.

games.title: Steps of an investigation
games.prompt: Put the steps in the usual order
items: Observe something and ask a question
Make a testable hypothesis
Plan and do an experiment
Record and analyse the data
Draw a conclusion and share it

games.title: Scientist or not?
items: A hypothesis must be something that can be tested.
If there is no way to test an idea, we cannot check whether it is correct.
If the results do not support your hypothesis, the experiment was useless.
Results that disagree with a hypothesis still teach us something and help us form a better hypothesis.
Repeating an experiment makes the results more reliable.
Repeating shows whether the result was a one-time accident or happens every time.
Scientists should change their data if it does not match what they expected.
Data must be reported honestly. Changing data is cheating and misleads everyone.
Observations can be made using our senses or using instruments like a thermometer.
Instruments help us observe and measure things our senses cannot measure exactly.

quiz.q: Which of these is a testable hypothesis?
options: Roses are the most beautiful flowers.
Salt water makes ice melt faster than plain water.
quiz.explain: We can test this by putting the same ice cubes in salt water and plain water and timing them. The other options are opinions that cannot be measured.
steps: A hypothesis must be testable: we must be able to measure or check it
Salt water versus plain water melting ice can be tested by timing identical ice cubes
'Most beautiful', 'fun' and 'boring' are opinions that cannot be measured
Answer: Salt water makes ice melt faster than plain water.
quiz.mistake: Confuses a personal opinion with a testable scientific idea

quiz.q: Meera notices that her bicycle tyre looks flatter in winter. What is this first step called?
quiz.explain: Noticing something with our senses is an observation. Investigations usually start with one.
steps: Meera noticed something using her senses
Noticing with the senses is an observation, the usual first step
A conclusion comes only at the end, after data
Answer: Observation
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the names of the steps of an investigation

quiz.q: Why should an experiment be repeated several times?
options: To make the result more reliable
So that the hypothesis is always proved right
quiz.explain: Repeating checks that the result was not just luck or a mistake in one trial.
steps: One trial may give a result by luck or by a small mistake
Repeating the test checks this and makes the result more reliable
Answer: To make the result more reliable
quiz.mistake: Thinks repeating an experiment is meant to force a particular answer

quiz.q: Kabir's results do not support his hypothesis. What should he do?
options: Accept the results and think of a new hypothesis to test
quiz.explain: Honest results that disagree with a hypothesis help us improve our idea. Science moves forward this way.
steps: Results that disagree with a hypothesis are still useful
Kabir should report them honestly and test a new hypothesis
Hiding or changing numbers is dishonest and stops learning
Answer: Accept the results and think of a new hypothesis to test
quiz.mistake: Believes an experiment fails if the hypothesis is not supported

options: The observations and measurements we record
The final opinion of the teacher
The list of materials we buy
quiz.explain: Data are the observations and measurements collected during an investigation, such as heights, times or temperatures.
steps: Data = the observations and measurements recorded during an investigation
e.g. heights, times or temperatures
Answer: The observations and measurements we record
quiz.mistake: Confuses data with the question or the conclusion

quiz.q: Which step comes right after making a hypothesis?
quiz.explain: Once we have a hypothesis, we design and carry out an experiment to test it.
steps: Order: observation and question → hypothesis → experiment → data → analysis → conclusion
So after the hypothesis comes testing it with an experiment
Answer: Testing it with an experiment
quiz.mistake: Does not know the order of the steps of an investigation

quiz.q: Why do scientists share their results with others?
options: So others can check and build on the work
So that nobody else ever tests it
Because sharing is a rule only for students
quiz.explain: When others repeat and check the work, mistakes are caught and knowledge grows.
steps: When others repeat and check the work, mistakes are caught
Others can also build on the results
Answer: So others can check and build on the work
quiz.mistake: Thinks science is done in secret by one person

quiz.q: Priya keeps a table of the daily temperature and the time milk takes to set into curd. Which step is she doing?
quiz.explain: Writing measurements in a table is recording data, which she will later analyse.
steps: Priya writes temperatures and setting times in a table
Writing measurements in a table is recording data
Answer: Recording data
quiz.mistake: Mixes up recording data with forming a hypothesis

teach.ask: Gappu chirps: I think my worms like the dark. How would a scientist check whether I am right?
teach.praise: Tweet! First a hypothesis, then a test, then look at the data. I am going to set up a worm experiment right now!
teach.nudge: But how do I actually find out? What do I do after guessing, and what do I write down?

revise.summary: Science starts with an observation and a question, then a testable hypothesis. We test it with a fair experiment, record data, analyse it, and change the hypothesis if needed, repeating and sharing results honestly.
focus: Order of the steps of an investigation
Telling a testable hypothesis from an opinion
What data is and why tests are repeated
Honest reporting and sharing of results
remember: Observation → question → hypothesis → experiment → data → analysis → conclusion
Hypothesis: a possible answer that can be tested
Data: the observations and measurements we record
traps: An opinion like 'roses are most beautiful' is not a testable hypothesis
Results that do not support a hypothesis are not failure — never hide or change them

learn.hook: Two friends race paper boats but one uses a bigger sheet AND blows harder. Who has the better design? Nobody can tell, because two things changed at once!
points: A variable is anything that can change in an experiment, such as temperature, amount of water or type of soil.
The independent variable is the one thing we change on purpose. The dependent variable is what we measure to see the effect.
Controlled variables are all the other things we keep the same so that the test is fair.
In a fair test we change only one variable at a time. Then any difference in results can be linked to that one change.
A control setup is kept without the change, so we can compare the results with it.

example.q: Think it through: Isha wants to know whether warm water makes sugar dissolve faster than cold water. What are her variables?
steps: What does she change on purpose? The temperature of the water, so that is the independent variable.
What does she measure? The time the sugar takes to dissolve, so that is the dependent variable.
What must stay the same? The amount of water, the amount and type of sugar, the glass and how she stirs. These are controlled variables.
example.answer: Independent: water temperature. Dependent: time to dissolve. Controlled: amount of water, amount and type of sugar, stirring and glass.

learn.reallife: When a cricket coach tests a new bat, players use the same ball and pitch so that only the bat is different. That is a fair test!

games.title: Which variable is it?
items: Amount of fertiliser given to each pot (testing fertiliser)
Height of each plant after 3 weeks
Type of seed in each pot
Amount of water each day
Size of each pot
Number of leaves on each plant

items.text: In a fair test, we change only ___ variable at a time.
The variable we measure is called the ___ variable.
Things we keep the same are called ___ variables.
A setup kept without the change, used for comparison, is called the ___.

quiz.q: Rohan tests whether the height of a ramp changes how far a toy car rolls. What is the independent variable?
quiz.explain: Rohan changes the ramp height on purpose, so it is the independent variable. The distance is what he measures.
steps: The independent variable is the one thing changed on purpose
Rohan changes the ramp height
So the ramp height is the independent variable; the distance is measured
Answer: Height of the ramp
quiz.mistake: Confuses the variable that is changed with the one that is measured

quiz.q: In the same ramp test, what is the dependent variable?
quiz.explain: The distance depends on the ramp height, and it is what Rohan measures.
steps: The dependent variable is what is measured to see the effect
Rohan measures how far the car rolls
So it is the distance the car rolls
Answer: Distance the car rolls
quiz.mistake: Picks the changed variable instead of the measured result

quiz.q: Why must we change only one variable at a time?
options: So that we know which change caused the result
So that results are always the same
quiz.explain: If two things change together, we cannot tell which one caused the difference in the results.
steps: If two things change together, we cannot tell which caused the result
Changing one variable at a time links the result to that one change
Answer: So that we know which change caused the result
quiz.mistake: Does not see that changing many things at once mixes up the causes

quiz.q: Neha tests which detergent removes a turmeric stain best. Which should she keep the SAME for every cloth?
options: The size of the stain and the washing time
quiz.explain: To be fair, only the detergent changes. Stain size, cloth, water and washing time must stay the same.
steps: Only the detergent should change
Everything else, like stain size, cloth, water and washing time, must stay the same
These are controlled variables
Answer: The size of the stain and the washing time
quiz.mistake: Thinks the variable being tested should also be kept the same

quiz.q: A student grows one plant with fertiliser and one plant without it. What is the plant without fertiliser called?
quiz.explain: The plant without the change is the control. We compare the fertilised plant with it.
steps: The plant kept without the change (no fertiliser) is used for comparison
A setup kept without the change is the control
Answer: The control
quiz.mistake: Does not know the meaning of a control setup

quiz.q: Which experiment is a fair test of whether sunlight helps seeds sprout?
options: One tray in sunlight with water, one tray in a dark cupboard without water
One tray in sunlight and one in the dark, both with the same water, soil and seeds
Two trays in sunlight with different seeds
One tray in the dark with more seeds
quiz.explain: Only the light is different, so any difference in sprouting can be linked to light.
steps: To test sunlight, only the light should differ
Water, soil and seeds must be the same in both trays
Option with water in only one tray changes two things, so it is unfair
Answer: One tray in sunlight and one in the dark, both with the same water, soil and seeds
quiz.mistake: Misses that water was also changed in the first setup

quiz.q: Anil wants to know if the mass of a pendulum bob affects how long one swing takes. Which is a controlled variable?
quiz.explain: He changes the mass and measures the swing time, so the string length must be kept the same.
steps: Anil changes the mass (independent) and measures the swing time (dependent)
Everything else must stay the same, such as the string length
So string length is a controlled variable
Answer: The length of the string
quiz.mistake: Picks the independent or dependent variable as a controlled one

quiz.q: Why do scientists usually test many seeds instead of just one in each tray?
options: One seed may behave unusually, so more seeds give a reliable result
More seeds make the experiment unfair
It is a rule that only big experiments count
quiz.explain: A single seed might be damaged. Using many seeds gives a result we can trust more.
steps: A single seed may be damaged or behave unusually
Many seeds give a result we can trust more
Answer: One seed may behave unusually, so more seeds give a reliable result
quiz.mistake: Does not understand why a larger sample makes results reliable

teach.ask: Gappu tilts his head: What makes an experiment a FAIR test? I changed everything at once and got confused!
teach.praise: Oh! Change just one thing, keep the rest the same, and measure the result. Now I can trust my tests!
teach.nudge: How many things should I change at a time? And what happens to all the other things?

revise.summary: In a fair test we change only one variable (independent), measure its effect (dependent) and keep everything else the same (controlled variables). A control setup without the change lets us compare results.
focus: Identifying independent, dependent and controlled variables
Why only one variable is changed at a time
Choosing a fair experiment and using many samples
remember: Independent variable: the one thing we change on purpose
Dependent variable: what we measure to see the effect
Controlled variables: everything else kept the same; control setup: kept without the change
traps: Don't mix up independent (changed) and dependent (measured) variables
Don't change two things at once — the test is no longer fair
